newMonitor.noticeDesc: Screen Tester provides visual inspection patterns and browser API observations. A web browser cannot determine true physical panel resolution, maximum physical refresh capability, actual nits brightness, actual contrast ratio, laboratory color accuracy (Delta E), true pixel response time, MPRT, input latency, panel health, remaining lifespan, internal electronics or capacitor condition, physical port solder integrity, guaranteed VRR hardware compliance, guaranteed HDR performance, or legal entitlement to a return or refund. This guide organizes your physical, visual, and browser-based observations.
newMonitor.policyNoticeTitle: Understanding Your Rights: Return Policy vs. Warranty vs. ISO Standards
newMonitor.policyNoticeDesc: Four distinct frameworks govern display purchases. They are not interchangeable:

policyItems.desc: The commercial return period offered by the seller (e.g. 14, 30 days depending on the retailer, seller, and purchase terms). This is typically the easiest window to return or exchange a monitor for any defect or dissatisfaction without undergoing complex manufacturer warranty procedures.

A separate limited warranty provided by the display brand (e.g. 1–3 years). It covers qualifying hardware defects under strict manufacturer criteria and usually involves repair or refurbishment rather than an immediate refund or brand-new exchange.

Legal protections established by regional laws (such as EU distance-selling consumer rights, UK Consumer Rights Act, or national commercial codes). These depend strictly on your country, jurisdiction, and purchase channel.

A technical benchmarking and classification framework for display pixel defects (typically Class I or Class II). ISO standards define manufacturing tolerances; they do NOT constitute consumer law and do NOT automatically guarantee a replacement or refund.

newMonitor.policyDisclaimer: Legal Disclaimer: Screen Tester does not provide legal advice. Return policies vary significantly by retailer, country, seller, and purchase method. Always verify the exact return window and warranty terms printed on your invoice or purchase agreement.
newMonitor.unboxingTitle: 1. Before Opening & Unboxing: Preserving Your Options
newMonitor.unboxingDesc: How you handle the initial package determines your return eligibility if damage occurred during shipping:

unboxingItems.title: Document Exterior Box Condition
unboxingItems.desc: Photograph all sides of the shipping carton before opening. Look for crushed corners, punctures, box tears, water stains, or resealed tape that could indicate transit damage or a refurbished/open-box return.

unboxingItems.title: Keep All Packaging, Inserts & Wraps
unboxingItems.desc: Never discard the outer carton, molded foam inserts, anti-static foam wraps, plastic cable bags, or protective peel-off films until your full inspection is complete and you have decided to keep the display. Many retailers reject returns or assess restocking fees for missing packaging.

unboxingItems.title: Verify Exact Model Number & SKU on Box Label
unboxingItems.desc: Check the exterior barcode sticker to verify the exact model suffix, panel type, and regional SKU. Retailers occasionally ship similar-sounding lower-tier variants (e.g., non-P or non-Ergo models) by mistake.

unboxingItems.title: Check Included Accessories & Documentation
unboxingItems.desc: Inventory the contents against the user manual: OEM external power adapter, power cord, DisplayPort cable, HDMI cable, USB-C upstream cable, stand base, screws, and factory calibration report (if applicable).

unboxingItems.title: Record Invoice & Determine Exact Return Deadline
unboxingItems.desc: Locate your digital order invoice or receipt. Identify the retailer's stated return/exchange window and calculate the exact calendar deadline. Set a reminder 3 to 4 days before this window closes.

newMonitor.physicalDesc: Perform a thorough visual inspection before plugging the monitor into electrical power:

physicalItems.title: Panel Surface & Coating Inspection
physicalItems.desc: Shine a smartphone light at a shallow 20° to 30° raking angle across the powered-off panel surface. Inspect for scratches, scuffs, gouges, or peeling anti-glare matte coating that can occur during factory assembly.

physicalItems.title: Edge, Corner & Bezel Integrity
physicalItems.desc: Inspect all four display corners and edges for micro-cracks or stress fractures in the glass substrate. Check that plastic bezel seams are evenly seated without loose snaps, bulging seams, or adhesive separation.

physicalItems.title: Stand Assembly & Ergonomic Adjustment
physicalItems.desc: Assemble the stand and test height, tilt, swivel, and pivot adjustments. Movements should be smooth with sufficient tension to hold position. If mounting to a monitor arm, check that VESA M4 screw threads are clean and unstripped.

physicalItems.title: Visual Port Inspection & Cable Fit
physicalItems.desc: Visually inspect HDMI, DisplayPort, USB-C, and power inputs for bent pins, debris, or damaged sockets before plugging in. Cables should insert cleanly without requiring excessive force.

physicalItems.title: Rattles, Loose Internal Parts & Odors
physicalItems.desc: Gently rotate the monitor upright; listen for loose screws or plastic clips rattling inside the housing. Check for severe chemical or burning odors from the rear vents. (Important: Never attempt disassembly or internal examination; inspect the exterior only).

newMonitor.powerDesc: Connect the display to AC power and observe initial startup behavior:

powerItems.title: Startup Latency & Power Indicator
powerItems.desc: Observe the power LED and display ignition. A new monitor should illuminate within 2 to 5 seconds. Persistent relay clicking, flickering standby LEDs, or failure to wake promptly indicates early power delivery instability.

powerItems.title: Immediate Signal Recognition & Image Stability
powerItems.desc: Connect your PC and verify that the screen displays a stable desktop image without unexpected flickering, image rolling, horizontal sync bars, or momentary blackouts during normal stationary operation.

powerItems.title: OSD Joystick & Button Responsiveness
powerItems.desc: Press the directional OSD joystick or chassis buttons. The on-screen display menu should open instantly and respond crisply to navigation inputs without sluggishness or ghost clicks.

powerItems.title: Brightness Adjustment & Inverter Stability
powerItems.desc: Cycle the monitor brightness slider in the OSD from 0% to 100%. Verify that dimming is smooth and continuous without high-pitched coil whine, buzzing, or sudden backlight shutdown.

newMonitor.pixelTitle: 4. Pixel Defect Inspection: Dead, Stuck & Hot Pixels
newMonitor.pixelDesc: Pixel anomalies are among the most common reasons for early returns. Open Screen Tester in fullscreen to thoroughly examine the matrix:

pixelItems.title: Dead Pixels (Dark on Bright Fields)
pixelItems.desc: Cycle through pure white, red, green, and blue backgrounds in the Dead Pixel Test. Dead subpixels remain permanently unpowered and appear as persistent dark specks against bright colors.

pixelItems.title: Stuck & Hot Pixels (Bright on Dark Fields)
pixelItems.desc: Open a solid black field in the Stuck Pixel Test. Transistors stuck in an energized state glow as persistent red, green, blue, or pure white (hot pixel) dots against black.

pixelItems.title: Dust Particle vs. True Pixel Defect
pixelItems.desc: Examine any pinpoint anomaly from a 45° side angle. If the dot shifts position relative to the illuminated pixel grid behind it and casts a shadow, it is trapped factory dust on the diffuser. If it sits squarely on the subpixel matrix, it is an electronic pixel defect.

pixelItems.title: Defect Eligibility & Warranty Reality
pixelItems.desc: Finding a single pixel defect does not automatically guarantee a manufacturer warranty replacement. Manufacturer RMA policies often require multiple dead or stuck pixels depending on cluster distance and ISO class. However, during your retailer return window, you can typically return or exchange the unit without satisfying manufacturer defect minimums.

newMonitor.imageDesc: Evaluate panel condition across uniform brightness, gradient reproduction, and text sharpness:

imageItems.title: Backlight Bleed vs. IPS Glow
imageItems.desc: Open the Backlight Bleed Test in a dimly lit room with a pure black background. Backlight bleed appears as localized yellow or white light pooling along bezel edges that stays fixed as you move your head. IPS glow appears as diffuse corner sheen that shifts in intensity and angle as your viewing position changes.

imageItems.title: Grayscale & Color Uniformity
imageItems.desc: Open the Uniformity Test with 50% neutral gray and pure white fields. Inspect for dirty screen effect (DSE), cloudy dark patches, vignetting at edges, or severe temperature splits (e.g. pink on the left, greenish on the right).

imageItems.title: Gradient Smoothness & Banding
imageItems.desc: Open the Gradient & Banding Test. Smooth grayscale gradients allow you to observe gradient transition quality and identify harsh staircase banding or visible stepping artifacts.

imageItems.title: Text Clarity & Subpixel Structure
imageItems.desc: Open the Text Clarity Test. Check for colored fringing on black text. Standard RGB layouts provide crisp rendering under standard OS ClearType/subpixel smoothing, while BGR or non-standard subpixel layouts may require software adjustments.

imageItems.title: Off-Axis Viewing Angle Shifts
imageItems.desc: Step 30° to 45° to the side and above the panel. IPS panels should maintain color consistency with minimal gamma shift. VA panels exhibit moderate shadow washout off-center, while TN panels show dramatic contrast inversion from below.

newMonitor.motionDesc: Verify that high-refresh gaming monitors deliver expected visual motion performance:

motionItems.title: Confirm Configured Refresh Rate in OS
motionItems.desc: New high-refresh monitors frequently default to 60Hz out of the box. Open your OS Advanced Display Settings and select the maximum rated refresh rate (e.g., 144Hz, 240Hz). Use Screen Tester's Refresh Rate Test to observe active frame cadence and detect obvious frame skipping.

motionItems.title: Ghosting & Pixel Response Trails
motionItems.desc: Open the Ghosting Test with moving high-contrast blocks. Visually observe whether trailing or smearing occurs behind moving objects. (Note: Visual motion patterns provide subjective observation of motion clarity; browser tools cannot measure true millisecond GtG transition times).

motionItems.title: Overdrive Tuning & Inverse Ghosting (Overshoot)
motionItems.desc: Cycle through your monitor's Overdrive/Response Time modes in the OSD (e.g. Off, Normal, Fast, Extreme). Extreme presets often create bright, glowing coronas (inverse ghosting/overshoot) behind moving objects; select the fastest setting that avoids noticeable coronas.

motionItems.title: VRR / Adaptive Sync & Brightness Flicker
motionItems.desc: Enable G-Sync Compatible or FreeSync in your GPU driver and test variable frame rate motion with the VRR Test. Watch for brightness flickering or micro-stuttering, particularly in near-black and fluctuating frame rate conditions.

newMonitor.osdDesc: Establish a clean baseline in the monitor's on-screen display menu:

osdItems.title: Confirm Input Signal & Resolution in OSD Info
osdItems.desc: Open the monitor's built-in OSD Information menu. Confirm that the incoming signal matches the panel's native resolution and intended refresh rate.

osdItems.title: Establish Default / Factory Preset Baseline
osdItems.desc: Start your testing from factory default settings or the Standard/sRGB picture preset. Disable aggressive dynamic contrast, non-standard sharpening filters, and extreme black equalizer levels before evaluating picture quality.

osdItems.title: Verify Color Profile & Color Space Modes
osdItems.desc: If your monitor features dedicated sRGB or DCI-P3 clamping modes, toggle them to confirm the OSD correctly locks or unlocks gamut controls without locking brightness to unusable levels.

osdItems.title: HDR Setting Verification (Where Supported)
osdItems.desc: If testing an HDR-capable monitor, toggle Windows/macOS HDR settings and inspect test patterns in the HDR Test. Note: Budget HDR400 displays without local dimming often produce washed-out SDR desktop images when HDR remains enabled.

newMonitor.osdNote: Note: A web browser cannot read internal monitor OSD registers or firmware settings directly. All OSD verification must be observed on the physical monitor menu.
newMonitor.portsTitle: 8. Physical Ports, USB Hubs & Cable Capabilities
newMonitor.portsDesc: Verify all physical connectors you intend to use before your return window closes:

portsItems.title: Test Every Video Input Independently
portsItems.desc: Connect your computer to each HDMI and DisplayPort socket on the rear panel. Switch inputs via the OSD to ensure every input scalar detects video cleanly.

portsItems.title: USB-C Features: Video vs. Charging vs. Data
portsItems.desc: Not all USB-C ports are identical. Verify whether your specific monitor model advertises DisplayPort Alt Mode (video transmission) and USB Power Delivery (laptop charging, e.g. 65W/90W). Test with a compatible, rated full-featured USB-C cable.

portsItems.title: USB Upstream & Downstream Hub Ports
portsItems.desc: Connect the monitor's USB upstream cable to your PC. Plug a flash drive or mouse into each downstream USB port to verify the hub controller operates without disconnection.

portsItems.title: Audio Passthrough & Headphone Jack
portsItems.desc: If your display includes a 3.5mm audio output or built-in speakers, select the monitor as your OS audio output and run Screen Tester's Speaker Test to verify left/right audio channels.

newMonitor.specialTitle: 9. Panel-Specific Checks: OLED vs. LCD Considerations
newMonitor.specialDesc: Different display panel technologies require specific quality observations:

specialItems.title: OLED: Near-Black Gradation & Gray Tinting
specialItems.desc: Open the Near-Black Test and inspect dark scenes for vertical banding, chrominance tint shifts, or crushed shadow details. OLED panels offer perfect blacks, but early near-black gray uniformity warrants verification.

specialItems.title: OLED: Panel Care & Automatic Maintenance Cycles
specialItems.desc: Familiarize yourself with your monitor's OLED care features (pixel shift, logo brightness limiter, and automatic pixel refresh). Understanding that short pixel-cleaning cycles run automatically upon standby prevents mistaking normal maintenance for a malfunction.

specialItems.title: LCD (IPS / VA / TN): Uniformity & Viewing Behavior
specialItems.desc: For LCD monitors, focus on edge-lit backlight uniformity, corner IPS glow distribution, and absence of vertical pressure marks caused by transit impacts on the bezel.

specialItems.title: Coating & Anti-Reflective Clarity
specialItems.desc: Inspect matte anti-glare coatings for excessive graininess ('sparkle') on pure white backgrounds, or glossy coatings for micro-scratches or uneven anti-reflective purple/blue reflections.

newMonitor.evidenceTitle: 10. Documenting Defects Before the Return Window Closes
newMonitor.evidenceDesc: If you discover an issue and need to contact the seller or manufacturer, clear documentation speeds up resolution:

evidenceItems.title: High-Quality Photos of Visible Defects
evidenceItems.desc: Take clear photos of physical damage, pixel defects, or severe backlight bleed. For pixel defects, capture both a wide shot showing the defect's location on the screen and a close-up photo.

evidenceItems.title: Short Video Demonstrating Intermittent Issues
evidenceItems.desc: If you experience flickering, blackouts, or strange OSD behavior, record a 10–15 second video on your smartphone clearly capturing the monitor screen, power LED, and cable connection simultaneously.

evidenceItems.title: Screenshot of OS Display Settings
evidenceItems.desc: Capture a screenshot of your OS Advanced Display Settings showing the active resolution, configured refresh rate, bit depth, and color format to confirm correct configuration.

evidenceItems.title: Save Barcode & Serial Number Details
evidenceItems.desc: Take a legible photo of the serial number sticker on the back of the monitor chassis and the matching barcode on the retail box.

newMonitor.evidenceDisclaimer: Important: Documenting an issue does not guarantee return approval or manufacturer warranty coverage. Always maintain genuine, unedited records.
newMonitor.decisionDesc: Use this structured evaluation to categorize your findings before your return deadline:

decisionCategories.normal: Flawless glass, intact bezels, smooth stand movement, clean ports.
decisionCategories.attention: Hairline scratch on frame, stiff pivot hinge, tight VESA screw.
decisionCategories.unsure: Crack in glass corner, bent port pin, rattling internal part.

decisionCategories.normal: Zero dead, stuck, or hot pixels across all primary colors.
decisionCategories.attention: Single stuck pixel in far peripheral corner; faint trapped dust speck.
decisionCategories.unsure: Multiple dead pixels clustered near screen center; bright hot pixel in primary view area.

decisionCategories.normal: Even illumination across gray fields; mild, symmetric IPS glow in corners.
decisionCategories.attention: Moderate backlight pinch on one bezel edge noticeable only on 100% black in pitch dark.
decisionCategories.unsure: Severe flashlighting visible in daylight desktop use; heavy pink/cyan tint split across panel.

decisionCategories.normal: Smooth motion at rated refresh rate; clean overdrive without severe halos.
decisionCategories.attention: Minor overshoot on aggressive overdrive preset (resolved by stepping down to Normal).
decisionCategories.unsure: Frequent frame skipping; aggressive black-smearing; VRR brightness flicker in desktop apps.

decisionCategories.normal: All inputs detect video quickly; stable power without buzzing or blackouts.
decisionCategories.attention: USB downstream port requires firm insertion; external power brick runs warm.
decisionCategories.unsure: Intermittent blackouts during stationary use; loud coil whine; USB-C fails to transmit video.

decisionCategories.normal: Invoice saved, packaging preserved, 7+ days remaining in retailer return window.
decisionCategories.attention: Retailer return window closes within 48 hours; decision required promptly.
decisionCategories.unsure: Return window already expired; issue must now proceed through manufacturer warranty/RMA.

newMonitor.actionTitle: 12. What to Do If You Find a Problem
newMonitor.actionDesc: Follow this logical sequence before initiating a return or warranty claim:
actionSteps: Step 1: Record and photograph the exact issue (photo or video showing context).
Step 2: Confirm the issue is reproducible across different cables, ports, or computers.
Step 3: Check OS display settings (resolution, refresh rate, scaling, HDR mode).
Step 4: Consult the monitor user manual to confirm expected hardware specifications.
Step 5: Check your retailer's applicable return/exchange policy and determine the exact return cutoff date.
Step 6: If within the retailer return window, initiating a seller exchange or return is typically faster than manufacturer warranty repair.
Step 7: If the retailer window has closed, check the manufacturer's warranty terms (RMA) and specific defect thresholds.
Step 8: Contact the appropriate seller or manufacturer customer support with your invoice and documentation ready.
newMonitor.quickChecklistDesc: A scannable pre-decision checklist for fast evaluation:
quickChecklist: Outer carton & packaging: all boxes, foam blocks, and wrappers kept in pristine condition.
Model SKU verified: barcode sticker on chassis matches the ordered model specifications.
Glass & coating: panel surface checked under raking light; zero scratches or coating abrasions.
Chassis & stand: bezels seated evenly; all stand adjustment axes smooth and stable.
First power-on: display boots cleanly within 2–5 seconds with stable backlight and power LED.
Pixel audit: Dead Pixel Test and Stuck Pixel Test completed across all solid background colors.
Backlight & uniformity: Backlight Bleed Test (black) and Uniformity Test (50% gray) inspected.
Motion & cadence: configured to maximum rated refresh rate in OS; tested in Refresh Rate Test.
Ports & connectivity: all required video inputs, USB-C capabilities, and hubs verified.
Return deadline: calendar reminder set before the retailer return/exchange window closes.
newMonitor.workflowCtaTitle: Ready for the interactive testing sequence?
newMonitor.workflowCtaDesc: Launch our guided New Monitor Inspection Workflow to step through dead pixel patterns, backlight checks, and uniformity sequences directly on your display.
newMonitor.description: A step-by-step practical guide to testing a newly delivered computer monitor for physical damage, pixel defects, panel uniformity, and motion performance before your retailer return window closes.

displayportVsHdmi.metaTitle: DisplayPort vs HDMI: Bandwidth, Revisions & Chroma Subsampling
displayportVsHdmi.metaDescription: In-depth guide to DisplayPort vs HDMI bandwidth, raw vs usable payload rates, protocol revisions (DP 1.4/2.1, HDMI 2.0/2.1), chroma subsampling (RGB vs 4:2:0), and resolving display bottlenecks.
displayportVsHdmi.title: DisplayPort vs HDMI: Bandwidth, Revisions & Chroma Subsampling
displayportVsHdmi.subtitle: A practical technical guide explaining raw vs usable bandwidth, protocol revisions, 4:4:4 vs 4:2:0 chroma subsampling, HDR transport, and resolving display pipeline bottlenecks.
displayportVsHdmi.honestyDesc: Screen Tester operates inside a standard web browser sandbox. Browser APIs can inspect viewport dimensions, frame dispatch cadence, and declared color gamuts, but cannot physically probe copper link signaling rates, cable impedance, GPU hardware PHY output stages, or internal Display Stream Compression (DSC) states. We distinguish four essential evaluation layers across this guide:

honestyItems.title: Claimed Hardware Standards
honestyItems.desc: The theoretical capabilities advertised on specification sheets (e.g., HDMI 2.1 48 Gbps or DisplayPort 1.4 HBR3). Actual hardware support depends on board layout, internal scaler chips, and controller firmware.

honestyItems.title: Negotiated Operating State
honestyItems.desc: The resolution, refresh rate, bit depth, and color format actively negotiated between your GPU driver and display EDID/DisplayID, visible in Windows Advanced Display Settings or GPU control panels.

honestyItems.title: Window & Render Context
honestyItems.desc: The dimensions, refresh cadence, and canvas color spaces directly exposed to web applications. A browser reporting 60 Hz or P3 color does not verify physical display hardware capabilities.

honestyItems.title: Perceptual Output Quality
honestyItems.desc: Observable artifacts such as text color fringing (chroma downsampling), gradient banding (8-bit vs 10-bit), micro-stutter, or blackouts caused by link signal degradation.

displayportVsHdmi.interfaceTitle: 1. What Each Interface Is: Architectural Lineage
displayportVsHdmi.interfaceDesc: DisplayPort and HDMI were created to solve different engineering challenges, resulting in distinct underlying signaling architectures:

interfaceItems.title: DisplayPort: The Open PC Standard
interfaceItems.desc: Developed by the Video Electronics Standards Association (VESA) as an open, royalty-free standard tailored specifically for personal computers. DisplayPort utilizes a packetized data architecture similar to PCI Express and Ethernet, transmitting micro-packets across 1, 2, or 4 high-speed differential data lanes. This packetized design makes DisplayPort natively adaptable to variable refresh rates, embedded display panels (eDP), and multi-display daisy-chaining (MST).

interfaceItems.title: HDMI: The Consumer Electronics AV Standard
interfaceItems.desc: Developed by an alliance of consumer electronics manufacturers (including Sony, Philips, Panasonic, and Toshiba) to connect televisions, AV receivers, set-top boxes, and gaming consoles. Traditionally built on Transition-Minimized Differential Signaling (TMDS) with three fixed data channels and a dedicated clock lane, HDMI evolved in version 2.1 to Fixed Rate Link (FRL)—adopting a packetized structure over 3 or 4 lanes to achieve higher bandwidth.

displayportVsHdmi.connectorTitle: 2. Why the Connector Alone Does NOT Determine Capability
displayportVsHdmi.connectorDesc: A common point of confusion is assuming that the physical shape of a port or cable guarantees bandwidth and feature support. Physical connector geometry does not dictate the underlying controller capability:

connectorItems.title: Branding Rules vs. Physical Ports
connectorItems.desc: Under official HDMI Forum licensing guidelines, devices are permitted to be labeled 'HDMI 2.1' even if they only support legacy HDMI 2.0 speeds (18 Gbps TMDS) without Fixed Rate Link (FRL), VRR, or eARC. Consumers must check the manufacturer's exact specification table for supported data rates rather than relying on the port label.

connectorItems.title: Internal Scaler & Timing Controller (T-Con) Limits
connectorItems.desc: A monitor may feature physical DisplayPort 1.4 or HDMI 2.1 jacks, but its internal scalar hardware, board routing, or firmware may cap maximum throughput to 24 Gbps or restrict 10-bit RGB color to lower refresh rates. The complete silicon pipeline dictates the actual limit.

displayportVsHdmi.hdmiRevisionsTitle: 3. HDMI Revisions: Protocol Standards & Real-World Modes
displayportVsHdmi.hdmiRevisionsDesc: HDMI has undergone significant architectural revisions. Supported modes depend entirely on whether the manufacturer implemented the full standard or a subset:

hdmiRevisionsItems.title: HDMI 1.4 (TMDS)
hdmiRevisionsItems.desc: Maximum raw link rate of 10.2 Gbps (usable payload ~8.16 Gbps via 8b/10b line coding). Supports 1080p up to 120Hz/144Hz and 4K up to 30Hz (or 4K 24Hz RGB). Inadequate for modern high-refresh 1440p or 4K HDR PC gaming.

hdmiRevisionsItems.title: HDMI 2.0 / 2.0b (TMDS)
hdmiRevisionsItems.desc: Maximum raw link rate of 18.0 Gbps (usable payload ~14.4 Gbps via 8b/10b line coding). Standardized 4K at 60Hz 8-bit RGB and 1440p up to 144Hz. Crucially, 4K 60Hz with 10-bit HDR exceeds 14.4 Gbps, forcing graphics cards to downsample chroma to YCbCr 4:2:2 or 4:2:0.

hdmiRevisionsItems.title: HDMI 2.1 / 2.1a (Fixed Rate Link - FRL)
hdmiRevisionsItems.desc: Replaces TMDS with FRL using efficient 16b/18b encoding (only ~11.1% overhead). Raw signaling rates range from FRL1 (9 Gbps) to FRL6 (48 Gbps raw / ~42.6 Gbps usable payload). Enables uncompressed 4K 120Hz 10-bit RGB, 8K 60Hz, and standardized HDMI VRR. Always verify the specific FRL rate supported by your display.

displayportVsHdmi.dpRevisionsDesc: DisplayPort scales bandwidth by increasing per-lane transmission frequency across four dedicated data lanes:

dpRevisionsItems.title: DisplayPort 1.2 (HBR2)
dpRevisionsItems.desc: High Bit Rate 2 mode delivers 21.6 Gbps raw across 4 lanes (usable payload ~17.28 Gbps using 8b/10b encoding). Supports 1080p 240Hz, 1440p 144Hz, and 4K 60Hz uncompressed 8-bit RGB. Standardized Multi-Stream Transport (MST) daisy-chaining.

dpRevisionsItems.title: DisplayPort 1.4 / 1.4a (HBR3)
dpRevisionsItems.desc: High Bit Rate 3 mode delivers 32.4 Gbps raw (usable payload ~25.92 Gbps using 8b/10b encoding). Introduces mandatory Display Stream Compression (DSC 1.2a) and HDR static metadata transport. Enables 1440p 240Hz uncompressed (8-bit) and 4K 144Hz (uncompressed 8-bit or 10-bit HDR via DSC).

dpRevisionsItems.title: DisplayPort 2.1 / 2.1a (UHBR)
dpRevisionsItems.desc: Ultra High Bit Rate modes introduce modern 128b/132b line coding (~97% efficiency). Includes UHBR10 (40 Gbps raw / 38.69 Gbps payload), UHBR13.5 (54 Gbps raw / 52.22 Gbps payload), and UHBR20 (80 Gbps raw / 77.37 Gbps payload). Capable of uncompressed 4K 240Hz 10-bit HDR, though display and GPU support remains model-specific.

displayportVsHdmi.bandwidthTitle: 5. Understanding Bandwidth: Raw Link Rate vs. Usable Payload
displayportVsHdmi.bandwidthDesc: Marketing materials frequently quote 'raw link rate', but display pipelines operate on 'usable payload bandwidth'. The difference is defined by line encoding and transport overhead:

bandwidthItems.title: Line Encoding Overhead (8b/10b vs 16b/18b vs 128b/132b)
bandwidthItems.desc: To ensure clock synchronization and maintain direct current (DC) balance, transmission protocols insert extra bits. Legacy 8b/10b encoding (HDMI 1.4/2.0, DP 1.2/1.4) converts every 8 bits of data into 10 transmitted bits, consuming 20% of raw bandwidth. HDMI 2.1 FRL uses 16b/18b encoding (11.1% loss), while DP 2.1 UHBR uses 128b/132b encoding (only ~3% loss).

bandwidthItems.title: Packet & Blanking Overhead
bandwidthItems.desc: Digital video streams require horizontal and vertical blanking intervals (front porch, back porch, sync pulses) to allow monitor timing controllers to reset between lines and frames. Auxiliary data packets, audio channels, and HDCP encryption metadata further reduce usable pixel throughput by approximately 3% to 8% depending on the video timing formula (e.g. standard CVT vs CVT-Reduced Blanking).

bandwidthItems.title: Real-World Usable Throughput Comparison
bandwidthItems.desc: Because of encoding differences, HDMI 2.0 (18 Gbps raw) yields ~14.4 Gbps usable payload. DisplayPort 1.4 (32.4 Gbps raw) yields ~25.92 Gbps usable payload. HDMI 2.1 FRL6 (48 Gbps raw) yields ~42.66 Gbps usable payload. DisplayPort 2.1 UHBR20 (80 Gbps raw) yields ~77.37 Gbps usable payload.

displayportVsHdmi.resRefreshDesc: Video bandwidth is governed by a fundamental formula: Width × Height × Refresh Rate (Hz) × Color Bit Depth × Color Multiplier + Blanking Overhead. Higher resolutions and frame rates scale bandwidth demands exponentially:

resRefreshItems.notes: Supported by HDMI 1.4 and DisplayPort 1.2 with substantial headroom. Well within legacy limits.
Fits within DisplayPort 1.2 (17.28 Gbps) and HDMI 2.0 (14.4 Gbps). Older HDMI 1.4 cannot support this rate.
Comfortably supported by DisplayPort 1.2/1.4. At the borderline of HDMI 2.0 capability (often requiring reduced blanking).
Exceeds uncompressed DisplayPort 1.4 (25.92 Gbps) and HDMI 2.0. Requires DisplayPort 1.4 with DSC or HDMI 2.1.
Standard for modern desktop monitors. Fits within HDMI 2.0 and DP 1.2. Cannot run 10-bit HDR on HDMI 2.0 without chroma subsampling.
Requires HDMI 2.1 (40/48 Gbps uncompressed) or DisplayPort 1.4 with DSC. Cannot run uncompressed over DP 1.4.
Exceeds all uncompressed links except DisplayPort 2.1 UHBR20. Relies on Display Stream Compression (DSC) across HDMI 2.1 and DP 1.4.

displayportVsHdmi.chromaTitle: 7. Chroma Subsampling: RGB vs. 4:4:4 vs. 4:2:2 vs. 4:2:0
displayportVsHdmi.chromaDesc: When available cable bandwidth is insufficient for a chosen resolution, refresh rate, and bit depth, graphics hardware must either lower the refresh rate or compress color data using chroma subsampling:

chromaItems.title: RGB & YCbCr 4:4:4 (Full Uncompressed Color)
chromaItems.desc: Every single pixel retains its own dedicated luminance (brightness) and chrominance (color) data. This is essential for PC monitors. Desktop operating systems rely on subpixel font rendering (e.g. Windows ClearType) where red, green, and blue subpixels are individually addressed to render crisp letterforms. Full 4:4:4 ensures razor-sharp text, UI borders, and fine line graphics.

chromaItems.title: YCbCr 4:2:2 (Horizontal Subsampling)
chromaItems.desc: Color resolution is halved horizontally while luminance remains full resolution. This saves approximately 33% of bandwidth. However, thin colored text, IDE code syntax highlights, and colored borders exhibit noticeable color bleeding, soft edges, and fringing artifacts.

chromaItems.title: YCbCr 4:2:0 (Horizontal & Vertical Subsampling)
chromaItems.desc: Color resolution is halved both horizontally and vertically, retaining only one color sample for every 2×2 block of pixels (50% bandwidth reduction). While 4:2:0 is the universal standard for video streaming, Blu-rays, and console gaming on distant TVs (where human visual acuity cannot resolve fine chroma detail), on a desktop computer at reading distance, 4:2:0 causes blurry, haloed, and distorted text.

displayportVsHdmi.chromaLinksTitle: Inspect Display Text Clarity & Subsampling Artifacts
displayportVsHdmi.bitDepthTitle: 8. Color Depth / Bit Depth: 8-Bit vs. 10-Bit Bandwidth Impact
displayportVsHdmi.bitDepthDesc: Bit depth defines the precision with which brightness steps are assigned to each color channel, with direct consequences for bandwidth consumption:

bitDepthItems.title: 8-Bit Color (16.7 Million Colors)
bitDepthItems.desc: Provides 256 gradations per RGB channel (2^8), totaling 24 bits per pixel (bpp). This is the traditional standard for SDR desktop computing and video. It requires the least bandwidth and is fully supported by all modern display protocols.

bitDepthItems.title: 10-Bit Color (1.07 Billion Colors)
bitDepthItems.desc: Provides 1,024 gradations per RGB channel (2^10), totaling 30 bits per pixel (bpp). 10-bit color requires exactly 25% more payload bandwidth than 8-bit color at the same resolution and refresh rate. It virtually eliminates color banding in smooth gradients and is the prerequisite for High Dynamic Range (HDR) standards.

bitDepthItems.title: 8-Bit + FRC (Frame Rate Control)
bitDepthItems.desc: Many displays market '1.07 billion colors' but physically use an 8-bit panel with temporal dithering (FRC), cycling adjacent subpixel colors rapidly between frames to simulate in-between shades. The GPU may transmit a native 10-bit signal across the cable (consuming 10-bit bandwidth), while the monitor's internal T-Con dithers it down to 8-bit.

displayportVsHdmi.hdrTitle: 9. The Complete HDR Signal Transport Chain
displayportVsHdmi.hdrDesc: High Dynamic Range (HDR) cannot be treated as an isolated display feature. It requires an unbroken transport chain across every link in your hardware setup:

hdrChainItems.desc: The graphics processor must support HDR static/dynamic metadata packet transmission (CTA-861-G / SMPTE ST 2086) over the active port controller.
The display stack must negotiate wide color gamut (typically Rec.2020 container) and enable 10-bit color depth in graphics control panels.
The link must have sufficient payload bandwidth to carry 10-bit color at the requested resolution and refresh rate without dropping into 4:2:0 subsampling.
The display's timing controller and backlight hardware must interpret metadata packets and provide meaningful peak luminance and local contrast control.

displayportVsHdmi.hdrLinksTitle: Evaluate Active HDR Capabilities & Dynamic Range
displayportVsHdmi.dscDesc: When physical interface bandwidth cannot meet the demands of modern high-resolution, high-refresh panels, the industry relies on VESA Display Stream Compression (DSC):

dscItems.title: What DSC Is
dscItems.desc: A VESA-standardized, low-latency, slice-based compression algorithm (DSC 1.2a) integrated into DisplayPort 1.4/2.1 and HDMI 2.1 pipelines. It operates in real time with virtually zero frame buffer latency (measured in microseconds, not milliseconds).

dscItems.title: Visually Lossless vs. Mathematically Lossless
dscItems.desc: DSC is mathematically lossy (typically operating at a 3:1 compression ratio), but has been rigorously tested through double-blind human perceptual evaluations to be visually lossless for realistic content, gaming, and typography.

dscItems.title: DSC Is Not 'Infinite Bandwidth'
dscItems.desc: DSC requires matching silicon support on both the GPU (Nvidia Turing or newer, AMD RDNA or newer, Intel Xe or newer) and the display scaler chip. If your GPU, dock, or KVM switch lacks DSC decoding, high-bandwidth combinations will fail to negotiate.

displayportVsHdmi.vrrTitle: 11. Variable Refresh Rate (VRR): Standards & Interface Nuances
displayportVsHdmi.vrrDesc: Smooth, tear-free gaming depends on Variable Refresh Rate, but the underlying protocols differ significantly across DisplayPort and HDMI:

vrrItems.title: VESA Adaptive-Sync (DisplayPort)
vrrItems.desc: The foundation for AMD FreeSync and Nvidia G-Sync Compatible on PC monitors. DisplayPort packetized timing enables seamless dynamic refresh rate modulation. Historically, Nvidia graphics cards only supported G-Sync Compatible over DisplayPort connections.

vrrItems.title: HDMI VRR (HDMI 2.1)
vrrItems.desc: Standardized in the HDMI 2.1 FRL specification. Widely supported on modern gaming televisions (LG OLED, Samsung, Sony) and consoles (PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X). Nvidia RTX 20/30/40/50 series GPUs support G-Sync Compatible over HDMI 2.1 VRR.

vrrItems.title: AMD FreeSync over HDMI (Legacy)
vrrItems.desc: A proprietary AMD vendor extension developed to enable variable refresh rates over legacy HDMI 1.4 and 2.0 connections. While supported by AMD Radeon GPUs, older Nvidia drivers frequently do not recognize G-Sync compatibility on monitors that only support FreeSync via HDMI.

displayportVsHdmi.vrrLinksTitle: Test Refresh Cadence & Variable Refresh Synchronization
displayportVsHdmi.cableDesc: High-frequency digital signals degrade rapidly over copper conductors. As data rates climb from 18 Gbps to 48 Gbps and 80 Gbps, cable construction becomes critical:

cableItems.title: Signal Attenuation Over Distance
cableItems.desc: Standard passive copper cables longer than 2 meters (6.6 feet) experience steep high-frequency signal loss at HDMI 2.1 (48 Gbps) or DP 2.1 (UHBR) speeds. For cable runs beyond 3 to 5 meters, active optical cables (AOC) with fiber-optic cores are frequently required.

cableItems.title: Official Certification Badges
cableItems.desc: Look for verified holographic certification labels: 'Ultra High Speed HDMI' (guaranteeing 48 Gbps FRL), 'Premium High Speed HDMI' (18 Gbps), or VESA-certified 'DP80' (80 Gbps) and 'DP40' (40 Gbps) logos. Uncertified generic cables are the primary source of intermittent dropouts.

cableItems.title: Physical Connector Integrity
cableItems.desc: Never subject video cables to sharp 90-degree bends near the connector strain relief. Do not apply bending force to ports while connected. Always secure monitor cables with appropriate slack to avoid port stress during height adjustments.

displayportVsHdmi.laptopDockTitle: 13. Laptops, USB-C DP Alt Mode, Docks & Adapters
displayportVsHdmi.laptopDockDesc: Connecting laptops through USB-C ports, multiport docks, and adapters introduces distinct architectural constraints:

laptopDockItems.title: USB-C DisplayPort Alternate Mode (2-Lane vs 4-Lane Split)
laptopDockItems.desc: A USB-C connector has 4 high-speed differential pairs. When connected directly to a monitor or portable display, all 4 lanes can carry DisplayPort video. However, when connecting through a multi-function USB-C dock that supports USB 3.0/3.2 data (5/10 Gbps), 2 lanes are reserved for USB data, leaving only 2 lanes for video—cutting available video bandwidth in half unless the dock utilizes DSC.

laptopDockItems.title: Multi-Stream Transport (MST) Daisy-Chaining
laptopDockItems.desc: DisplayPort allows daisy-chaining multiple monitors over a single physical cable using MST. All connected displays share the single port's total payload bandwidth. Crucially, macOS does NOT support MST daisy-chaining (all chained displays mirror the same desktop image); Windows and Linux fully support extended MST multi-monitor setups.

laptopDockItems.title: Active vs. Passive Adapters & Converters
laptopDockItems.desc: DisplayPort can output HDMI signals through passive adapters (DP++) only up to legacy HDMI 1.4/2.0 speeds. Converting HDMI to DisplayPort or adapting HDMI 2.1 requires an active converter powered by USB. These active adapters frequently disable VRR, increase input latency, and complicate HDR handshakes.

displayportVsHdmi.determineTitle: 14. How to Determine What Your Specific Setup Supports
displayportVsHdmi.determineDesc: Follow this methodical sequence to identify the true capabilities of your display hardware pipeline:
determineSteps: Step 1: Consult your GPU specification sheet to verify output port revisions (e.g. DP 1.4a vs DP 2.1, HDMI 2.0b vs HDMI 2.1 FRL rate) and DSC architecture support.

Step 2: Read your monitor's technical manual to determine which specific physical ports support maximum bandwidth (e.g. HDMI 1 may be 2.0 while HDMI 2 is 2.1, or high refresh may be exclusive to DisplayPort).
Step 3: Check OS Display Settings (Windows Settings → System → Display → Advanced Display) to inspect current active signal resolution, refresh rate, and color bit depth.

Step 4: Open your GPU Control Panel (NVIDIA Control Panel → Change Resolution, AMD Software → Display, or Intel Graphics Command Center) to inspect and configure output color format (RGB vs YCbCr444/422/420) and output dynamic range.
Step 5: Verify that your video cable carries official certification for the target bandwidth tier, avoiding unrated generic adapters.
displayportVsHdmi.troubleshootDesc: When video signal handshakes fail or bandwidth thresholds are exceeded, specific symptoms emerge across your display pipeline:

troubleshootScenarios.title: Black Screen or Intermittent Signal Dropouts (Flicker Under Load)
troubleshootScenarios.symptom: Display works at desktop but goes black intermittently when launching full-screen games or switching to 120Hz/144Hz.
troubleshootScenarios.cause: Cable bandwidth insufficiency or high-frequency attenuation. The physical link cannot sustain high bitrates without packet corruption.
troubleshootScenarios.fix: Shorten cable length (under 2m / 6ft), replace with an officially certified cable, or slightly reduce refresh rate to verify stability.

troubleshootScenarios.title: Missing High Refresh-Rate Options in OS Settings
troubleshootScenarios.symptom: Windows or macOS only lists refresh rates up to 60Hz or 100Hz on a 144Hz/240Hz gaming monitor.
troubleshootScenarios.cause: Connected via an HDMI port that is limited to HDMI 2.0 or 1.4 speeds, or connected through a dock with 2-lane DP bandwidth constraints.
troubleshootScenarios.fix: Switch from HDMI to DisplayPort, enable high-refresh mode in the monitor's built-in OSD menu, or connect directly to the laptop's dedicated GPU port.

troubleshootScenarios.title: HDR Toggle Greyed Out or Washes Out Desktop Colors
troubleshootScenarios.symptom: Windows HDR toggle cannot be enabled, or enabling HDR results in dull, grey, washed-out SDR colors.
troubleshootScenarios.cause: Inadequate link bandwidth to negotiate 10-bit color, or monitor lacks local dimming / wide color gamut mapping on the current input.
troubleshootScenarios.fix: Ensure the port is set to PC/Enhanced mode in monitor OSD, switch to DisplayPort, and verify bit depth is set to 10-bit in GPU control panel.

troubleshootScenarios.title: Forced YCbCr 4:2:2 or 4:2:0 (Text Fringing & Bleeding)
troubleshootScenarios.symptom: GPU control panel forces YCbCr422 or 420; RGB 4:4:4 is not selectable; small text shows color fringing.
troubleshootScenarios.cause: The chosen resolution, refresh rate, and 10-bit color exceed the maximum uncompressed payload of the port without DSC.
troubleshootScenarios.fix: Reduce refresh rate by one step, switch from 10-bit to 8-bit color for SDR desktop work, or upgrade to DisplayPort 1.4 / HDMI 2.1.

troubleshootScenarios.title: VRR / G-Sync Compatible Option Missing from GPU Driver
troubleshootScenarios.symptom: Nvidia Control Panel lacks the 'Set up G-SYNC' menu item, or AMD FreeSync reports unsupported.
troubleshootScenarios.cause: Connecting an Nvidia graphics card via HDMI to a monitor that only supports FreeSync over HDMI or DisplayPort Adaptive-Sync.
troubleshootScenarios.fix: Connect via DisplayPort. For modern TVs, ensure HDMI 2.1 VRR and Game Mode are enabled in the TV's external input settings.

troubleshootScenarios.title: Display Functions Only at Lower Resolution or Lower Refresh
troubleshootScenarios.symptom: Monitor operates at 1080p instead of 4K, or 4K only at 30Hz.
troubleshootScenarios.cause: Connected through a legacy HDMI 1.4 port or a non-compliant passive dongle/adapter.
troubleshootScenarios.fix: Inspect the monitor user manual to identify the full-speed input port, remove passive adapters, and connect directly to the primary GPU output.

displayportVsHdmi.decisionTitle: 16. Practical Decision Framework: When to Choose DP vs. HDMI
displayportVsHdmi.decisionDesc: Use this practical decision matrix to select the optimal interface based on your specific display and source hardware:

decisionMatrix.useCase: PC Gaming on a High-Refresh Monitor
decisionMatrix.why: Guarantees full G-Sync Compatible and FreeSync compatibility, eliminates chroma downsampling, and supports maximum refresh rates on virtually all PC gaming monitors.

decisionMatrix.useCase: PC Connected to a Modern 4K/120Hz Television
decisionMatrix.why: Modern OLED and Mini-LED TVs do not feature DisplayPort inputs; HDMI 2.1 delivers full 4K 120Hz/144Hz 10-bit RGB with standardized HDMI VRR.
Consoles exclusively feature HDMI outputs and require HDMI 2.1 for 4K 120Hz, Variable Refresh Rate (VRR), and Auto Low Latency Mode (ALLM).
Enables connecting multiple monitors sequentially from a single GPU output port, drastically simplifying cable management.
Native DisplayPort transport delivers superior multi-display bandwidth and DSC support through modern Thunderbolt and USB4 docks.

decisionMatrix.useCase: Home Theater AV Receiver or Soundbar Setup
decisionMatrix.why: HDMI is the universal standard for carrying multi-channel uncompressed surround audio (Dolby Atmos, DTS:X) via enhanced Audio Return Channel.

monitorOsdSettings.metaTitle: Monitor OSD Settings Explained: Overdrive, HDR, VRR & More
monitorOsdSettings.metaDescription: Practical guide to monitor on-screen display (OSD) settings: learn what overdrive, MBR, VRR, HDR, gamma, local dimming, and sharpness actually change, and how to visually verify them.
monitorOsdSettings.title: Monitor OSD Settings Explained
monitorOsdSettings.subtitle: A practical technical guide explaining what on-screen display controls alter, how to balance motion clarity and color accuracy, manufacturer quirks, and how to verify settings using visual browser tests.
monitorOsdSettings.honestyDesc: Screen Tester operates inside a standard web browser sandbox. Web APIs can inspect viewport dimensions, canvas color spaces, and animation frame dispatch cadences, but cannot physically measure monitor backlight nits, sensor-calibrated Delta E, pixel response times in milliseconds, or physical VRR frequency ranges. To evaluate your display accurately, we distinguish six critical evaluation layers across this guide:

honestyItems.title: Firmware Hardware Registers
honestyItems.desc: Internal scaler controls stored in the monitor EEPROM/NVRAM, adjusted via physical buttons or directional joystick independent of the operating system.

honestyItems.title: System Display Pipeline
honestyItems.desc: The resolution, refresh rate, desktop scaling factor, and color profile requested by Windows, macOS, or Linux display settings.

honestyItems.title: Graphics Control Panel
honestyItems.desc: Output dynamic range (RGB Full vs Limited), color format (RGB vs YCbCr), scaling modes, and sync behavior set in Nvidia, AMD, or Intel drivers.

honestyItems.title: Render Context Timings
honestyItems.desc: Viewport dimensions, device pixel ratio, and requestAnimationFrame intervals exposed to web applications. Browser timing does not prove physical panel limits.

honestyItems.title: Perceptual Evaluation
honestyItems.desc: Direct visual inspection of observable artifacts such as ghosting trails, overshoot coronas, text fringing, gradient steps, and brightness uniformity.

honestyItems.title: Advertised Lab Metrics
honestyItems.desc: Marketing numbers (e.g. '0.5ms GtG', '1000 nits peak', '3000:1 contrast') measured under aggressive lab testing conditions that rarely reflect real-world default use.

monitorOsdSettings.whatIsOsdDesc: The On-Screen Display (OSD) is the monitor's embedded firmware interface rendered directly by the display's internal scaler and timing controller (T-Con). Navigated with physical buttons, a directional joystick, or companion software (via DDC/CI), it controls hardware-level panel functions independently of your computer.

whatIsOsdItems.title: Independent Scaler Execution
whatIsOsdItems.desc: The OSD is rendered internally by the monitor's scaler processor. It overlays directly on screen even when no video cable is connected or the operating system is completely unresponsive.

whatIsOsdItems.title: Manufacturer Naming Chaos
whatIsOsdItems.desc: The same underlying feature carries radically different marketing names across brands: Overdrive is called 'Trace Free' by ASUS, 'AMA' by BenQ, and 'Response Time' by LG and Samsung.

whatIsOsdItems.title: Context-Dependent Locks
whatIsOsdItems.desc: Many OSD controls are conditionally locked out. Enabling an sRGB picture preset or HDR mode often grays out Brightness, Contrast, Color Temperature, and Overdrive settings.

whatIsOsdItems.title: Non-Standardized Presets
whatIsOsdItems.desc: Identical setting names can behave completely differently across monitors. 'Fast' overdrive on one panel may provide crisp motion, while on another it introduces unbearable overshoot halos.

monitorOsdSettings.brightnessContrastTitle: 2. Brightness and Contrast: What They Actually Control
monitorOsdSettings.brightnessContrastDesc: Brightness and Contrast are the two most frequently adjusted controls, yet they are widely misunderstood. Understanding their underlying digital and hardware behavior prevents severe image degradation.

brightnessContrastItems.title: Brightness: Backlight Luminance
brightnessContrastItems.desc: Adjusts the physical power delivery to the LED backlight (or OLED pixel emission). It controls overall display luminance without altering the digital RGB code values of your content. Always adjust Brightness to match ambient room lighting (comfortable lower levels in dim environments, higher in daylight) rather than setting an arbitrary extreme level. Browser JavaScript cannot physically measure optical luminance.

brightnessContrastItems.title: Contrast: Digital White-Point Mapping
brightnessContrastItems.desc: Controls the digital scaling of input RGB values. On digital inputs (DisplayPort and HDMI), setting Contrast above the factory default forces digital highlight clipping, collapsing near-white tones (e.g., IRE 240–255) into a blown-out white sheet.

brightnessContrastItems.title: Testing Baseline & Verification
brightnessContrastItems.desc: Keep Contrast at factory default (typically 50 or 70 depending on model). Use the Gradient Banding Test and White-Level Test to verify that grayscale ramps step smoothly without clipped highlight bands.

monitorOsdSettings.overdriveDesc: Overdrive (voltage boost) is the single most critical setting for gaming motion clarity on LCD displays. It accelerates liquid crystal physical rotation to shorten Gray-to-Gray (GtG) transition times.

overdriveItems.title: The Fundamental Trade-off: Ghosting vs. Overshoot
overdriveItems.desc: If overdrive is too low, liquid crystals turn too slowly, leaving visible trails and smearing (ghosting) behind moving objects. If overdrive voltage is pushed too high, crystals shoot past their target color, producing bright or dark glowing halos (inverse ghosting or overshoot coronas).

overdriveItems.title: Marketing Traps: '0.5ms' and 'Extreme' Presets
overdriveItems.desc: Manufacturer specification sheets advertise '1ms' or '0.5ms' GtG response times that can only be achieved on the highest, most aggressive overdrive preset (e.g., 'Extreme' or 'Fastest'). In real-world gaming, this setting produces severe, distracting inverse ghosting and is practically unusable.

overdriveItems.title: Variable Refresh Rate (VRR) Interaction
overdriveItems.desc: Unless a monitor features sophisticated dynamic or variable overdrive (common in hardware G-Sync modules), a fixed overdrive setting tuned for 180 Hz will produce severe overshoot when in-game framerates drop down to 60–80 Hz.

overdriveItems.title: Recommended Visual Testing
overdriveItems.desc: Start at the medium preset ('Fast', 'Normal', or Level 2). Launch the Screen Tester Ghosting Test and Motion Blur Test at your typical gaming refresh rate to visually find the sweet spot between trailing and halos.

monitorOsdSettings.mbrDesc: Motion Blur Reduction (MBR)—also branded as ULMB, ELMB, DyAc, PureXP, Aim Stabilizer, or 1ms MPRT—reduces perceived motion blur by strobing the backlight in synchronization with the refresh cycle.

mbrItems.title: How Strobing Combats Eye-Tracking Blur
mbrItems.desc: Modern flat panels are sample-and-hold displays: each frame remains illuminated continuously until the next refresh. As human eyes track moving objects across the screen, this persistence causes retinal blur. Strobing turns the backlight off while pixels transition and pulses it on only when pixels are stable, dramatically improving perceived motion sharpness.

mbrItems.title: The Severe Trade-offs: Brightness & Flicker
mbrItems.desc: Because the backlight is turned off for a large portion of each frame interval, overall screen luminance drops significantly (often by 30% to 50%). Furthermore, rapid strobing creates noticeable flicker that can cause eye strain, headaches, and fatigue during long sessions.

mbrItems.title: VRR and Strobe Crosstalk Conflicts
mbrItems.desc: On most monitors, enabling MBR automatically disables Adaptive Sync / VRR, requiring a rock-solid framerate matching the monitor refresh rate to prevent stutter. Strobe timing differences across the panel can also produce 'strobe crosstalk' (double imaging at the top or bottom of the screen).

mbrItems.title: Testing Recommendation
mbrItems.desc: Compare moving objects in the Motion Blur Test with MBR toggled on and off. Keep MBR disabled for desktop productivity, general gaming, and content creation, reserving it only for fast-paced competitive esports.

monitorOsdSettings.vrrDesc: Variable Refresh Rate (VRR)—standardized across VESA Adaptive-Sync, AMD FreeSync, and Nvidia G-Sync Compatible—dynamically synchronizes the monitor refresh cycle to the GPU's instantaneous frame delivery rate.

vrrItems.title: Eliminating Tearing Without VSync Stutter
vrrItems.desc: Traditional fixed refresh rates cause either horizontal tearing (VSync Off) when frames arrive mid-scan, or severe stutter and input lag (VSync On) when a frame misses the refresh deadline. VRR eliminates tearing while preserving ultra-low input latency across variable framerates.

vrrItems.title: The Complete Hardware & Software Chain
vrrItems.desc: VRR requires seamless cooperation across the entire display pipeline: GPU driver setting, DisplayPort or HDMI 2.1 cable bandwidth, operating system variable refresh toggle, and the monitor OSD toggle. If any single link in the chain is disabled, VRR will not engage.

vrrItems.title: LFC & Brightness Flickering Gotchas
vrrItems.desc: If framerate drops below the monitor's minimum VRR threshold (e.g. 48 Hz), Low Framerate Compensation (LFC) duplicates frames. On some VA and OLED panels, large framerate fluctuations cause subtle gamma shifts, perceived as rapid brightness flickering in dark scenes.

vrrItems.title: Browser Testing Scope
vrrItems.desc: The Screen Tester VRR Test allows visual observation of smooth motion and tearing elimination. However, browser JavaScript cannot certify hardware G-Sync hardware modules or verify the physical minimum/maximum Hz boundaries of the panel.

monitorOsdSettings.hdrDesc: High Dynamic Range (HDR) expands contrast and color volume. However, turning on the 'HDR' setting in a monitor OSD is frequently misunderstood by consumers.

hdrItems.title: Signaling Support vs. True Panel Capability
hdrItems.desc: An OSD setting labeled 'HDR: On' merely allows the monitor scaler to accept an HDR10/PQ signal from Windows or your console. It does NOT magically grant the physical display hardware the high peak luminance, wide color gamut, or localized contrast necessary for true HDR presentation.

hdrItems.title: The Budget Edge-Lit HDR Trap
hdrItems.desc: On standard edge-lit LCD monitors with global dimming and modest peak brightness, enabling HDR frequently degrades the image: black levels are raised to a muddy gray, SDR desktop content looks washed out, and the OSD typically locks out user brightness and color adjustments.

hdrItems.title: When HDR is Genuinely Worthwhile
hdrItems.desc: HDR delivers genuine visual impact primarily on displays equipped with per-pixel luminance control (OLED / QD-OLED) or multi-hundred-zone Full-Array Local Dimming (Mini-LED) where specular highlights can achieve high luminance alongside deep, uncompromised blacks.

hdrItems.title: Visual Testing in Browser
hdrItems.desc: Open the Screen Tester HDR Test. Verify whether your browser and operating system successfully negotiate high dynamic range canvas drawing without highlight clipping or SDR color space distortion.

monitorOsdSettings.gammaTitle: 7. Gamma Settings: Presets and Tonal Curves
monitorOsdSettings.gammaDesc: Gamma governs the mathematical curve that translates digital color values into actual perceived luminance, having its most pronounced impact on midtone brightness.

gammaItems.title: Standard Targets: Gamma 2.2 and sRGB
gammaItems.desc: For PC gaming, digital video, and web browsing, Gamma 2.2 (or the closely matching sRGB transfer curve) is the universal industry standard. It ensures that midtones appear with the exact luminance balance intended by game developers and content creators.

gammaItems.title: Effects of Gamma Deviations
gammaItems.desc: Setting gamma too low (e.g. 1.8 or 2.0) lifts midtones excessively, making the entire screen look washed out, pale, and hazy. Setting gamma too high (e.g. 2.4 or 2.6) darkens midtones, causing 'black crush' where subtle shadow textures are swallowed into total blackness.

gammaItems.title: Manufacturer Preset Inaccuracies
gammaItems.desc: OSD gamma labels ('1.8', '2.0', '2.2', '2.4') are often poorly calibrated from the factory. A preset labeled '2.2' may actually track at 2.05 or 2.35 on a specific panel. Always test using gradient patterns rather than blindly trusting the menu label.

gammaItems.title: Testing with Screen Tester
gammaItems.desc: Evaluate your gamma setting using our Gradient Banding and Near-Black tests to ensure smooth, step-free gradation between deep shadows and bright midtones.

monitorOsdSettings.colorTempTitle: 8. Color Temperature and RGB Gain Controls
monitorOsdSettings.colorTempDesc: Color Temperature controls the chromaticity of the display's white point, while RGB Gain allows granular adjustments to individual red, green, and blue color channels.

colorTempItems.title: Targeting D65 / 6500K Neutral White
colorTempItems.desc: The international digital imaging standard is D65 (approximately 6500 Kelvin). OSD presets labeled 'Warm' often align closest to 6500K, whereas 'Normal' or 'Cool' typically boost blue channel output (7500K–9000K) to create an artificially piercing, clinical white.

colorTempItems.title: RGB Gain Sliders: Channel Balancing
colorTempItems.desc: Selecting 'User' or 'Custom' unlocks separate Red, Green, and Blue gain sliders. These allow you to eliminate subtle tinting (e.g., dialing down Green if the white point looks sickly, or trimming Blue if it looks icy).

colorTempItems.title: The Danger of Over-Clipping RGB Gains
colorTempItems.desc: Adjusting RGB gains without a hardware spectrophotometer is subjective. Setting any channel above its factory maximum causes digital clipping (highlight discoloration), while lowering all three excessively reduces maximum peak brightness.

colorTempItems.title: Visual Uniformity Verification
colorTempItems.desc: Inspect a pure full-screen white canvas on the Uniformity Test to verify that your white point appears neutral and free of distracting color casts across the panel surface.

monitorOsdSettings.sharpnessTitle: 9. Sharpness: Edge Enhancement vs. Native Resolution
monitorOsdSettings.sharpnessDesc: Sharpness is one of the most frequently abused monitor OSD settings. On modern digital displays, it is an artificial edge-enhancement filter.

sharpnessItems.title: It Does NOT Increase Resolution
sharpnessItems.desc: Sharpness processing cannot add physical pixels or real detail to a panel. A 2560×1440 monitor has exactly 3,686,400 physical pixels regardless of whether sharpness is set to 0% or 100%.

sharpnessItems.title: Artificial Ringing and Halos
sharpnessItems.desc: Increasing sharpness above the neutral baseline applies high-frequency spatial filtering, creating glaring white halos (ringing artifacts) around text glyphs and fine lines. This reduces readability and degrades font rendering.

sharpnessItems.title: The Neutral Baseline Rule
sharpnessItems.desc: When transmitting digital video (DisplayPort or HDMI) at the monitor's native panel resolution, the correct setting is the neutral bypass position (usually 50% or 0 depending on brand). Only legacy analogue or heavily upscaled content ever benefits from sharpening.

sharpnessItems.title: Verifying with Text Clarity Test
sharpnessItems.desc: Open the Screen Tester Text Clarity Test at 100% scale. Adjust sharpness until high-contrast black text on white displays sharp, legible edges without any surrounding white halos or blurred fringes.

monitorOsdSettings.localDimmingDesc: Available on premium LCD displays with Full-Array Local Dimming (FALD) or Mini-LED backlights, this setting controls how actively individual backlight zones brighten and dim.

localDimmingItems.title: Zone Contrast Modulation
localDimmingItems.desc: Standard LCDs illuminate the entire screen with a global backlight. Local dimming divides the backlight into dozens, hundreds, or thousands of discrete physical zones, dimming dark areas to achieve deep blacks while driving bright highlights to maximum output.

localDimmingItems.title: The Blooming / Haloing Trade-off
localDimmingItems.desc: When a small bright element (such as mouse cursor or subtitles) appears against a black background, light leaks into the surrounding dimmed zones, producing visible glowing halos ('blooming'). More aggressive local dimming reduces blooming but may crush subtle starfields or dark details.

localDimmingItems.title: Desktop vs. Gaming Use Cases
localDimmingItems.desc: During desktop productivity, rapid zone switching around scrolling text can be distracting. Many users prefer setting Local Dimming to 'Low' or 'Off' for desktop work, switching to 'High' for HDR gaming and movies.

localDimmingItems.title: Testing Zone Behavior
localDimmingItems.desc: Use the Near-Black and Uniformity tests to visually observe how local dimming zones behave under moving high-contrast elements.

monitorOsdSettings.blackEqualizerTitle: 11. Black Equalizer / Shadow Boost / Dark Boost
monitorOsdSettings.blackEqualizerDesc: Popular on competitive gaming monitors, Black Equalizer (also known as Black eQualizer, Shadow Boost, or Dark Stabilizer) alters near-black gamma curves.

blackEqualizerItems.title: Competitive Utility in Esports
blackEqualizerItems.desc: By aggressively lifting the lowest 0–20% luminance values without altering midtone and highlight brightness, this feature makes enemies hiding in dark corners instantly visible in titles like Counter-Strike or Rainbow Six.

blackEqualizerItems.title: Severe Impact on Visual Fidelity
blackEqualizerItems.desc: Shadow boosting severely distorts creator intent. Contrast is gutted, atmospheric darkness is washed out into pale gray, and compression artifacts in shadows become glaringly visible. It should always be set to neutral for movies and story-driven games.

blackEqualizerItems.title: Visual Calibration with Near-Black Test
blackEqualizerItems.desc: Launch the Near-Black Test. Verify that subtle low-IRE patches are distinguishable from true black without washing out the entire dark field into noisy gray.

monitorOsdSettings.refreshRateDesc: Some gaming monitors expose refresh rate toggles, overclock profiles (e.g. 144 Hz to 180 Hz), or active timing displays directly within the OSD menu.

refreshRateItems.title: Distinguishing the Four Frequency Layers
refreshRateItems.desc: A monitor OSD displaying '180 Hz' simply indicates that an internal overclock register is enabled. If Windows or your GPU driver is set to 144 Hz, your desktop and games will run strictly at 144 Hz. Furthermore, browser JavaScript reporting 144 Hz only reflects DOM animation frame cadence, not physical panel hardware certification.

refreshRateItems.title: Overclock Stability & Frame Skipping
refreshRateItems.desc: Pushing panel overclocking toggles in the OSD can sometimes cause subtle frame skipping, visual artifacts, or thermal degradation over time. Always test an overclocked refresh rate for dropped frames.

refreshRateItems.title: Cable Bandwidth Verification
refreshRateItems.desc: Enabling higher refresh rates often exhausts cable throughput, forcing graphics drivers to automatically drop color bit-depth from 10-bit to 8-bit or downsample chroma from RGB to 4:2:2 or 4:2:0.

refreshRateItems.title: Testing with Refresh Rate & Motion Tests
refreshRateItems.desc: Validate active refresh timing with Screen Tester's Refresh Rate Test and inspect motion fluidness on the Motion Blur Test.

monitorOsdSettings.aspectRatioTitle: 13. Aspect Ratio and Scaling Modes in OSD
monitorOsdSettings.aspectRatioDesc: Dictates how the monitor's internal scaler handles video signals that do not match the panel's physical aspect ratio or native pixel grid.

aspectRatioItems.title: Full Screen vs. Aspect vs. 1:1 Pixel Mapping
aspectRatioItems.desc: 'Full Screen' stretches any input signal to fill the panel, distorting non-native aspect ratios. 'Aspect' scales the image up to the maximum dimension while preserving correct proportions with black bars (pillarboxing/letterboxing). '1:1' (Dot-by-Dot) displays the incoming resolution without any scaling, mapping each input pixel directly to one physical panel pixel.

aspectRatioItems.title: Monitor Scaler vs. GPU Scaler
aspectRatioItems.desc: Scaling can be performed by either the monitor's onboard scaler or your graphics card GPU (configured via Nvidia Control Panel or AMD Radeon Software). Modern GPUs typically offer superior scaling algorithms (such as integer scaling for retro pixel art) and lower latency than cheap monitor scaler chips.

aspectRatioItems.title: Visual Verification
aspectRatioItems.desc: Use the Screen Tester Scaling & Aspect Ratio Test and Display Info tool to verify that non-native resolutions retain correct geometry and crisp pixel boundaries.

monitorOsdSettings.factoryResetDesc: The 'Reset' or 'Recall' function clears user modifications stored in the monitor's firmware and restores factory default calibration values.

factoryResetItems.title: What Factory Reset Actually Does
factoryResetItems.desc: Over months of tweaking, overlapping picture modes, custom RGB gains, and aggressive overdrive settings can produce visual degradation that is difficult to isolate. A factory reset restores the firmware configuration back to its baseline out-of-the-box state.

factoryResetItems.title: What It CANNOT Fix
factoryResetItems.desc: Factory reset cannot repair physical panel defects, dead or stuck pixels, mechanical pressure marks, backlight bleed, torn ribbon cables, or failing LED driver boards. Do not expect firmware resets to cure hardware faults.

factoryResetItems.title: When to Use It
factoryResetItems.desc: Perform a factory reset when unboxing a newly purchased monitor, before testing a second-hand display, or whenever unexplained color banding, tinting, or input lockouts occur.

monitorOsdSettings.baselineDesc: When tuning monitor settings, follow this disciplined 7-step evaluation protocol. Note: Screen Tester visual patterns help evaluate visible artifacts and perceptual behavior under controlled conditions; they do not directly measure or certify underlying hardware electronic registers or optical luminance.
baselineSteps: 1. Record current OSD state: Document all existing picture profiles, color gains, and feature toggles before making any changes.
2. Establish a baseline: Set native resolution, native refresh rate, and standard/neutral picture mode with comfortable brightness matched to ambient light.
3. Change ONE setting at a time: Modify a single setting by one increment or profile level to isolate its specific visual effect.
4. Re-run the relevant Screen Tester test: Open the corresponding test pattern designed for that visual dimension.
5. Compare before/after visually: Inspect for changes in trailing smearing, overshoot halos, edge ringing, or color balance under identical viewing conditions.
6. Record the setting and observed effect: Note the setting value and whether it improved clarity, introduced artifacts, or caused regressions.
7. Restore preferred settings afterward: Keep the optimal setting or restore your previous baseline if the adjustment produced visual degradation.
monitorOsdSettings.testingMatrixDesc: Display calibration is an iterative process. Change exactly one OSD setting at a time, then immediately run the corresponding visual test to evaluate the real-world perceptual result.

testingMatrixRows.goal: Check for trailing smearing (too low) vs glowing overshoot halos/coronas (too high).
Evaluate retinal motion clarity vs flicker fatigue and screen dimming.
Observe smooth animation cadence and absence of horizontal tearing lines.
Verify highlight gradient transitions and inspect whether SDR desktop contrast is preserved.
Confirm frame dispatch cadence and test for stutter or skipped frames.
Ensure text edges are crisp and readable without artificial white halos or blurring.
Check for smooth tonal steps across 256 grayscale levels without harsh banding lines.
Ensure low-IRE dark shades are distinguishable without turning pure black into milky gray.
Inspect full-screen white field for clean, neutral white balance without color casts.
Observe zone blooming halos and dark-scene light leakage under moving high-contrast elements.
Verify non-native resolutions retain correct proportions and pixel geometry.

monitorOsdSettings.mistakesDesc: Avoid these widespread configuration pitfalls that degrade image quality and motion clarity:

mistakesItems.title: Selecting 'Fastest' Overdrive Blindly
mistakesItems.desc: Manufacturers label the most extreme overdrive setting 'Fastest' or '1ms' for marketing compliance. In reality, it delivers immense voltage spikes resulting in unplayable overshoot coronas. The middle setting is almost always superior.

mistakesItems.title: Cranking Contrast to 100%
mistakesItems.desc: Users often increase contrast hoping for 'punchier' images. On digital displays, this crushes near-white highlights into blown-out flat white, erasing fine textures in skies, clouds, and bright surfaces.

mistakesItems.title: Enabling HDR on Budget Edge-Lit Monitors
mistakesItems.desc: Running HDR on entry-level displays (DisplayHDR 400 with global dimming) often causes washed-out desktop colors, elevated black levels, and locked-out OSD controls with zero true HDR contrast benefit.

mistakesItems.title: Leaving Sharpness Too High
mistakesItems.desc: Excessive sharpness does not add real detail; it adds glaring white halos around letters that cause eye fatigue and blurry text edges. Keep sharpness at the neutral baseline.

mistakesItems.title: Using 'FPS' or 'Vivid' Presets Everywhere
mistakesItems.desc: Game presets heavily distort color saturation and gamma to reveal enemies in shadows. While useful in esports, they ruin color balance and contrast for casual gaming, video watching, and office work.

mistakesItems.title: Ignoring OSD Control Lockouts
mistakesItems.desc: Selecting certain picture modes (e.g. sRGB emulation) often locks brightness or color controls. If an OSD slider is grayed out, check whether a restrictive picture preset or HDR mode is active.

monitorOsdSettings.limitationsDesc: Screen Tester provides powerful visual observation patterns, but users must understand what web browser technologies can and cannot physically measure:

limitationsItems.title: No Physical Luminance (Nits) Sensor
limitationsItems.desc: A web browser operates strictly in software; it has no optical sensor to measure real-world candelas per square meter (cd/m² or nits) emitted by your backlight.

limitationsItems.title: No Spectrophotometric Delta E Measurement
limitationsItems.desc: Evaluating color accuracy and true Delta E requires a physical colorimeter or spectrophotometer coupled with direct sensor profiling software.

limitationsItems.title: Visual Observation vs. Lab Response Times
limitationsItems.desc: Screen Tester's Ghosting and Motion Blur tests provide human visual patterns to identify trailing and overshoot coronas. They do not calculate millisecond GtG transition graphs, which require high-speed photodiode oscilloscopes.

limitationsItems.title: No Hardware VRR Certification
limitationsItems.desc: Our VRR test validates visual tear-free rendering and frame pacing, but cannot certify internal hardware G-Sync module presence or query the panel's physical scalar firmware frequency limits.

monitorOsdSettings.troubleshootDesc: If your monitor exhibits persistent visual anomalies such as flickering, signal loss, unresolvable color tints, or locked OSD menus after adjustment, explore our dedicated display troubleshooting guide for step-by-step diagnostic workflows.

Privacy.metaDescription: Monitor Tester privacy policy: All tests execute locally in your browser. Zero telemetry, zero analytics tracking, and zero remote storage.
Privacy.title: Privacy Policy
Privacy.description: Monitor Tester is designed with a strict privacy-first architecture. All display diagnostic tests and calculations execute entirely inside your local browser.
Privacy.noCollectionText: When you visit Monitor Tester and run display tests, we do NOT collect, transmit, or store any personal data, hardware serial numbers, diagnostic observations, or screen metrics on external servers. There are no backend tracking databases, user accounts, or login requirements.
Privacy.localStorageText: To provide convenient features such as checklist tracking and defect marker coordinates, Monitor Tester utilizes your browser's private local storage APIs:
Privacy.localStorageItem1: Active Session & Observations (localStorage): Stores your self-reported test ratings (Pass, Check, Issue), custom notes, and pixel defect pin coordinates (X/Y pixels) so your report remains accessible if you refresh the page.
Privacy.localStorageItem2: Workflow Queue (sessionStorage): Temporarily keeps track of your current step in guided inspection workflows (e.g., General Checkup or Used Monitor Inspection). This is automatically cleared when you close your browser tab.
Privacy.localStorageClear: You can clear all stored data at any time by clicking 'Reset' in the test runner, clearing your browser's site data, or using your browser's private / incognito browsing mode.
Privacy.cookiesText: Monitor Tester does not use third-party advertising cookies, behavioral trackers, or marketing pixels. The site does not sell, rent, or monetize your browsing activity.
Privacy.permissionsText: Monitor Tester requests only the standard Fullscreen API permission when you choose to enter full-screen testing mode. Fullscreen requires an explicit user gesture (such as clicking the Fullscreen button or pressing 'F') as enforced by your browser. We never request camera, microphone, notification, or geographic location permissions.
Privacy.workflowStorageDesc: Temporarily tracks your current test index during multi-step inspection workflows. This is purged automatically when you close the tab.
Privacy.questionsDesc: Contact our open-source maintainers or review the source code directly.

About.metaDescription: Learn about Monitor Tester, a free browser-based suite designed to test, inspect, and diagnose computer monitors, laptops, TVs, and mobile displays.
About.title: About Monitor Tester
About.description: A free, privacy-first browser utility built to evaluate, inspect, and troubleshoot computer monitors, laptops, mobile devices, and TVs without software installation.
About.missionText: Buying a new or used monitor often involves uncertainty: dead pixels, backlight bleed, washed-out contrast, and ghosting are difficult to identify during brief in-store checks or unboxings. Monitor Tester was created to provide a complete, accessible suite of diagnostic patterns that anyone can run immediately in any modern web browser.
About.howItWorksText: Every test runs locally on your device using standard HTML5 Canvas, WebGL, CSS hardware acceleration, and the Screen and Window APIs. No downloads, native installers, or administrative permissions are needed. Your display data stays entirely on your computer.
About.pixelsDesc: Detect dead pixels, stuck subpixels, bright subpixels, and panel image retention (burn-in) across pure color fields.
About.colorDesc: Evaluate continuous gradients, color banding steps, color gamut boundaries, and multi-step grayscale ramps.
About.luminanceDesc: Tune near-black and near-white clipping, check dark-room backlight bleeding, and assess full-screen brightness uniformity.
About.motionDesc: Check ghosting trails, evaluate pixel overdrive settings, measure V-Sync refresh rate (Hz), and inspect for screen tearing.
About.toolsDesc: Inspect detected screen metrics (DPR, color depth), calculate PPI and optimal viewing distances, compare displays, and test multi-touch.
About.openSourceText: Monitor Tester is an open-source project. You can inspect the source code, report rendering bugs, suggest new test patterns, or contribute directly on GitHub.
